Abstract:
Phase microscopy allows stain-free imaging of transparent biological samples. One technique, using the transport of intensity equation (TIE), can be performed without dedicated hardware by simply processing pairs of images taken at known spacings within the sample. The resulting TIE images are quantitative phase maps of unstained biological samples. Therefore, spatially resolved optical path length (OPL) information can also be determined. Using low-cost, open-source hardware, we applied the TIE to living algal cells to measure their effect on OPL. We obtained OPL values that were repeatable within species and differed by distinct amounts depending on the species being measured. We suggest TIE imaging as a method of discrimination between different algal species and, potentially, non-biological materials, based on refractive index/OPL. Potential applications in biogeochemical modelling and climate sciences are suggested.

Abstract:
This article presents a review after an exhaustive search that yielded 23 works carried out in the last decade for the availability of optical microscopes with open hardware as a low‐cost alternative to commercial systems. These works were developed with the aim of covering needs within several areas such as: Bio Sciences research in institutions with limited resources, diagnosis of diseases and health screenings in large populations in developing countries, and training in educational contexts with a need for high availability of equipment and low replacement cost. The analysis of the selected works allows us to classify the analyzed solutions into two main categories, for which their essential characteristics are enumerated: portable field microscopes and multipurpose automated microscopes. Moreover, this work includes a discussion on the degree of maturity of the solutions in terms of the adoption of practices aligned with the development of Open Science.

Abstract Premise Low‐cost, repairable lab equipment is rare within the biological sciences. By lowering the costs of entry using 3D printing and open‐source hardware, our goal is to empower both amateur and professional scientists to conduct research. Methods We developed a modular system of 3D‐printable designs called COBLE (Collection of Bespoke Laboratory Equipment), including novel and remixed 3D‐printable lab equipment that can be inexpensively printed, assembled, and repaired for a fraction of the cost of retail equivalents. Results Here we present novel tools that utilize 3D printing to enable a wide range of scientific experiments. We include additional resources for scientists and labs that are interested in utilizing 3D printing for their research. Discussion By describing the broad potential that 3D‐printed designs can have in the biological sciences, we hope to inspire others to implement and improve upon these designs, improving accessibility and enabling science for all.

Abstract:
Nowadays, many industries use robots and cameras in tandem to detect specific objects and perform specific tasks. However, misdetection can occur due to inconsistencies in lighting, background, and environment. In order to address the aforementioned issues, this study proposes using a dual arm six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) collaborative robot, ABB YuMi, and red, green, blue-depth (RGB-D) camera with YOLOv5 in a pick-and-place application. In order to prepare the dataset, the images are collected and labeled. The dataset has been trained with the YOLOv5 machine learning algorithm. It has taken on the role of weight for real-time detection. When RGB images from a camera are sent to YOLOv5, data pertaining to the bottle’s position x-y and color are extracted from the depth and color images. The position of the robot is used to control its movement. There are three parts to the experiment. To begin, YOLOv5 is tested with and without trained images. Second, YOLOv5 is tested with real-time camera images. Finally, we assume that YOLOv5 has perfect detection and grasping ability. The results were 95, 90, and 90%.

Abstract:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been explored and verified to be effective in solving decision-making tasks in various domains, such as robotics, transportation, recommender systems, etc. It learns from the interaction with environments and updates the policy using the collected experience. However, due to the limited real-world data and unbearable consequences of taking detrimental actions, the learning of RL policy is mainly restricted within the simulators. This practice guarantees safety in learning but introduces an inevitable sim-to-real gap in terms of deployment, thus causing degraded performance and risks in execution. There are attempts to solve the sim-to-real problems from different domains with various techniques, especially in the era with emerging techniques such as large foundations or language models that have cast light on the sim-to-real. This survey paper, to the best of our knowledge, is the first taxonomy that formally frames the sim-to-real techniques from key elements of the Markov Decision Process (State, Action, Transition, and Reward). Based on the framework, we cover comprehensive literature from the classic to the most advanced methods including the sim-to-real techniques empowered by foundation models, and we also discuss the specialties that are worth attention in different domains of sim-to-real problems. Then we summarize the formal evaluation process of sim-to-real performance with accessible code or benchmarks. The challenges and opportunities are also presented to encourage future exploration of this direction. We are actively maintaining a repository to include the most up-to-date sim-to-real research work to help domain researchers.

This is a Research and Development (R&D) with the ADDIE model where  12 active students of chemistry department involved at the implementation stage. Data was collected through interview, questionnaire of need analysis and questionnaires to seek the opinion from students, laboratory assistant and lecturer. It was revealed that the student worksheet was valid with score of validity of 97,8%, thus, applicable for investigation. Response of students, laboratory assistants and lecturers to the implementation of practicum using student worksheet which has been developed as a whole is very good. 47,92% student were strongly agreed about practicum relevancy to daily life, 50% agreed that inquiry questions are useful. 75% of assistants strongly agreed that worksheet can help students to design their own experiments and 25% agreed about demanded the ability of class management. 71,43% lecturers strongly agreed that worksheet can motivate students to be more active and 28,57% agreed that worksheet is effective to achieve the practicum objectives. Jenis penelitian yang digunakan adalah Research and Development (R&D) dengan model ADDIE. Subjek penelitian tahap implementasi adalah mahasiswa aktif pendidikan kimia berjumlah 12 orang. Pengumpulan data diperoleh dari wawancara, angket analisis kebutuhan serta angket respon dari praktikan, asisten laboratorium dan dosen. Hasil penelitian ini menunjukkan bahwa persentase rata-rata kelayakan LKM yang divalidasi tim ahli oleh dosen dan penilaian oleh asisten laboratorium adalah 97,8%, dan dapat dikategorikan sangat valid dan layak digunakan tanpa revisi. Persentase rata-rata respon dosen adalah 71,43% sangat setuju bahwa LKM mampu memotivasi praktikan lebih aktif dan 28,57% setuju bahwa LKM efektif dalam mencapai tujuan praktikum. Abstract:
The Covid-19 pandemic highlighted infection and hygiene as risks in dense public spaces, including public transport vehicles. This study investigated passenger touching behaviour within metro vehicles to understand the fomite exposure of passengers. Using in-vehicle CCTV on three lines of the London Underground, this paper investigated the number of touches on different types of train interiors and investigated their relationship with passenger density and movement. In total, 1,818 station sections and 16,891 passengers were observed cumulatively from May to December 2021. The results showed that on average for each type of interiors on Victoria and Jubilee lines, there were between 0.07 to 0.57 touches per passenger movement (i.e. boarding or alighting) for deep tube lines, whilst District line that uses larger carriages showed a different tendency. The results also suggested that for deep tube lines, the number of touches per person increased beyond a density of around 1.5 standing passengers per square meter possibly because passengers may touch interiors more in order not to bump into other passengers. These findings can be used in infection risk modelling and can inform mitigation of infection risk of future pandemics. Highlights • Investigated passenger touching behaviour on train interiors within metro vehicles. • On average there were between 0.07 to 0.57 touches per passenger movement (i.e. boarding or alighting). • The number of touches per person increased beyond a density of around 1.5 standing passengers per square meter. • These findings can be used in infection risk modelling and inform mitigation of fomite infection risk of future pandemics.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (1632–1723) transformed observation into science through the power of a single handmade lens. His work emerged from the visual culture of seventeenth-century Delft, where craftsmanship, optics, and artistic precision intersected. While Robert Hooke’s compound microscope introduced the idea of microscopic visualization, Leeuwenhoek’s single-lens instruments achieved far superior magnification and resolution by minimizing optical interfaces. Using these deceptively simple devices, he documented the first observations of free-living microorganisms, fungal hyphae, red blood cells, capillary flow, oral bacteria, and spermatozoa in more than two hundred letters to the Royal Society of London.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>But his investigations reached far beyond microbiology. Leeuwenhoek also examined the barbed structure of the bee sting, the ordered vessels of ash wood, and the geometric microstructure of crystals and salts—demonstrating that hidden organization pervades both living and non-living matter. These studies established microscopy as a universal investigative tool, capable of unifying biology, medicine, botany, and early materials science under a single optical principle.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Leeuwenhoek’s work marks one of the earliest examples of how rigorous observation can redefine scientific domains. His use of a home-crafted single lens created an empirical foundation for biological microscopy that persists to this day. The legacy of his minimalist optical design also survives in the digital age: modern clip-on smartphone microscopes and paper-based platforms such as the Foldscope reproduce the same single-lens principle through micro-optics mounted directly onto digital sensors.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Three and a half centuries later, his work continues to remind us that new worlds do not emerge from new theories alone, but from new ways of seeing.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The escalating global environmental crisis highlights the need for effective conservation models, a gap addressed by analyzing indigenous knowledge systems. This study’s objective was to investigate and analyze the ethnoforestry principles and practices of the Baduy community in Banten, Indonesia, focusing on their contribution to the sustainable conservation of forests and water resources. Employing a qualitative ethnographic approach, data were gathered in Kanekes village through in-depth interviews with customary leaders (Pu'un), participant observation, and documentation of customary laws (pikukuh). The findings reveal a sophisticated ethnoforestry system rooted in the pikukuh customary law, which strictly delineates forest zones into protected (leuweung kolot) and agricultural (huma) areas. This classification governs resource extraction and ensures the preservation of core ecosystem functions. Crucially, water management is intrinsically linked to forest protection, preserving the Ciujung watershed’s quality. The novelty lies in empirically documenting this successful indigenous system. The implication is that the Baduy’s integration of spiritual beliefs with ecological principles offers a proven, replicable model for sustainable development, underscoring the vital importance of incorporating local wisdom into contemporary environmental governance and policy-making.</jats:p>

Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mempertegas dan memperjelas bahwa penelitian menggunakan model PjBL-STEM memberikan dampak positif dalam pembelajaran. Metode penelitian menggunakan Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dimana peneliti mengkaji atau mereview 72 artikel dari beberapa jurnal melalui database Scopus dengan rentangan tahun 2018-2022. Pengambilan data melalui teori Inklusi dan Eksklusi sehingga hasil akhir artikel yang didapatkan sebanyak 40 artikel open access dengan database scopus. Model PjBL yang dipadukan dengan pendekatan STEM merupakan langkah inovatif dalam pembelajaran yang memberikan kesempatan peserta didik untuk merencanakan proses pembelajaran secara kolaboratif dan menghasilkan suatu produk tertentu yang digunakan sebagai sumber belajarnya. Berdasarkan hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa PjBL-STEM memiliki dampak positif dalam dunia pendidikan. Diantaranya melalui PjBL-STEM mampu meningkatkan keterampilan pemecahan masalah, mampu meningkatkan literasi, mampu meningkatkan self-efficacy, mampu meningkatkan hasil belajar peserta didik serta membuat peserta didik tertarik dalam menuju karir dan profesi STEM karena peserta didik belajar dengan menyenangkan dan pembelajaran yang disampaikan bermakna (meaningful learning). Kemampuan dari dampak positif inilah yang nantinya sebagai bekal peserta didik dalam mengembangkan keterampilan abad ke-21.
 
Systematic literature review: Project-based learning integrated with STEM
 
Abstract: The study aims to emphasize and clarify that research using the PjBL-STEM model has a positive impact on learning. The research method uses Systematic Literature Review (SLR) where researchers study or review 72 articles from several journals through the Scopus database with a range of years 2018-2022. Data collection was done through inclusion and exclusion theory so that the final results of articles were obtained from as many as 40 open-access articles with Scopus databases. The PjBL model combined with the STEM approach is an innovative step in learning that gives students the opportunity to plan the learning process collaboratively and produce a specific product that is used as a learning resource. Among them, PjBL-STEM can improve problem-solving skills, can improve literacy, can increase self-efficacy, is able to improve the learning outcomes of pupils, as well as make pupils interested in the direction of careers and STEM profession because pupils learn with fun and learning delivered meaningful (meaningful learning). The ability of this positive impact will be the future supply of students in developing the skills of the 21st century.

                  <jats:p>Numerous activities in the plant sciences require time‐consuming, repetitive actions that are ideal for automation, but existing tools to accomplish these types of tasks are often priced beyond the reach of many research labs, especially in low‐resource environments. We developed a suite of easy‐to‐use, three‐dimensional (3D)‐printable tools for seed handling, tissue collection, and bead dispensing. The designs were made using accessible software and tested for speed and accuracy across multiple crops. Compared to commercial and manual methods, the 3D‐printed tools were significantly faster with comparable or superior accuracy. Costs of printed tools were 0.1%–21% of commercial equivalents. All designs are freely available online and can be easily adjusted to suit different research needs or printer types. Inexpensive, open‐source hardware can meaningfully increase throughput, standardization, and reproducibility in plant research, especially for programs operating under budget constraints.</jats:p>

3. Organization of a distributed project
Managing and directing a distributed, open project requires active collaboration and network-
ing; the publication of source code and designs is only the first step in making the project
accessible. How to best manage a collaborative project is both a technical and social problem,
as users require both technical skills and motivation to share their work. Any barrier to the free
sharing of knowledge and experience can decrease the effectiveness of a project.

(a) Capturing an evolving design

Documentation of the design, decisions and knowledge of a project is key to OpenFlexure
development for two reasons. First, medical certification requires an archive of decisions,
allowing the project history to be traced. Second, as an open-source project, designs are released
in the hope that users can build, use and modify the design without requiring direct contact
with the original development team.
   Capturing the decisions and discussions of a multinational evolving team is non-trivial,
and requires tools developed for supporting collaboration. OpenFlexure version control is
performed in Git, a distributed system primarily used for software development. While GitLab
hosts the OpenFlexure software, including the server, GUI and calibration procedures, it also
hosts the microscope CAD files, acting as a version control system for an evolving hardware
design.
   While GitLab—as a public forum for discussion—is preferred by the core development
team for its archiving, traceability and openness, feedback from some collaborators suggests apreference for communication through private channels such as WhatsApp or email. Whether                                                                                                            7
due to protecting intellectual property, being unwilling to publicly share suggestions or
preferring the wider use of these platforms, this moves some discussion and decisions into
private channels. The project will often benefit from the core development team publicly
recording the outcomes of these conversations at a later date. Otherwise, there is significant
risk of replicating previous work, discussion or mistakes.

We have described the considerations and challenges involved in turning an academic
prototype into a medical device for global health. Some of these considerations are specific
for microscopy, while others apply generally to improving the accessibility of healthcare. This
development extends beyond purely technical challenges; the project requires acceptance from
clinicians to test, feedback on and use the device.
   This development has surpassed the typical scope of an academic project—the further
release of manufacturing-ready designs, technical documentation and support are all required

academic researchers, it benefits from the involvement of the original core team [24].

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Commercialization of academic open-source laboratory hardware

**The documented pathway is to publish a reproducible design while selling the things that publication does not supply:** manufactured and tested instruments, convenient kits, specialist components, integration, training, and dependable support. Openness permits competing manufacturers; it does not eliminate customers’ willingness to pay for an instrument that works on arrival. Evidence of commercial *activity* is considerably stronger than evidence of company revenue or profit for individual academic projects. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010)

The cases below distinguish reported sales from self-builds, prices, manufacturing costs, and plans.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## Pathways and observed outcomes

**Product companies and local manufacture.** OpenFlexure Industries is listed as a manufacturer of the OpenFlexure microscope and block stage. Separately, Tanzanian partner Bongo Tech and Research Labs manufactures an OpenFlexure-derived **sayansiScope** and was working toward medical-device certification in the 2024 account. OpenFlexure had been built or used in **more than 45 countries** and had reached **technology-readiness level 7**, including operational testing with patient samples; neither figure is a sales total. The cited material does not establish that either manufacturer is a *formal university spinout*, nor disclose its revenue. Other documented product businesses include Opentrons, openUC2 and Sci-Bots, which is listed for the DropBot digital-microfluidics controller. These are examples of commercialization around open designs, not evidence that all have the same institutional ownership or licensing arrangement. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000055)

**Assembled robots and application-specific integration.** An early Opentrons **OT.One was listed at US$3,000**; that is a product price, *not* Opentrons revenue. During the COVID-19 response, an account reported an Opentrons-supported workflow developed with diagnostic partners for **up to 2,400 tests per day**, associated with US FDA emergency-use authorization, and reported automation at Barcelona’s Hospital Clínic diagnostic centre. The regulatory claim concerns that testing workflow; it should not be read as approval of every use of an open pipetting robot. An academic lab can also publish a liquid handler without establishing a seller: PHIL, FINDUS and OpenWorkstation document buildable laboratory-automation designs, but their reported prototype or component costs are not evidence of commercial sales. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050)

**Kit sellers, component suppliers and distributors.** Imperial College London’s **openFrame** team worked with Cairn Research Ltd; its paper states that Cairn **would sell** openFrame components to users who want to assemble instruments but not fabricate the components. This documents a stated supplier route, not a measured volume of completed sales. The paper estimates **under £10,000** in components for some self-assembled bright-field or fluorescence configurations and approximately **£35,000** for its motorized easySTORM configuration, excluding a computer; both are *assembly-cost estimates*. Jubilee illustrates a transition from sourcing parts from numerous vendors to a complete kit offered by a US vendor in February 2022. Its **170 independently built machines** by then establish uptake before the kit launch, not 170 kit sales. More generally, LabMaker and Adafruit are identified as vendors of designs developed by others; marketplaces and resellers—including Tindie and, in broader open-hardware examples, MatterHackers and Adafruit—can provide distribution without acquiring exclusive design rights. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

**Crowdfunded small batches and educational kits.** The University of Utah’s open **CLSLab:Light** self-driving-laboratory teaching demonstrator went beyond a downloadable design: the authors report **two successful GroupGets rounds totaling 39 kits**, some used in university teaching. Their April 2023 disclosure gives a **US$80 list price plus shipping**, **US$51.19 hardware**, **US$15.57 platform fees**, about **US$6 labor/testing**, and approximately **US$2.24 profit per kit** before the effects of bulk discounts. These are unusually transparent *per-kit figures*, not annual revenue. The wider literature identifies crowdfunding as a way to finance pre-sales and test demand, and group purchasing as a means of reducing small-batch production risk; neither guarantees a scalable business. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039)

**High-volume manufacture is possible, but projections must stay projections.** Stanford-origin Foldscope provides a different scale of example. Manu Prakash reported in 2017 that **50,000 microscopes had been made and sold**; his statement that the team *would ship one million that year*, and a separately reported million-device distribution goal, are **targets or forecasts**, not independently verified million-unit sales. The reported **less-than-US$1 production cost** likewise is not a sale price or revenue. Federal funding supported its early pilot. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000025)

**Institutional licensing and industry co-development.** The CERN Open Hardware Repository shows a transfer route in which companies help develop or manufacture openly documented designs and the research institution serves as an initial customer and quality signal. CERN reported that, by the end of **2014**, **eight CERN designs were commercially available** and **more than 1,200 units** had been produced for almost **100 users**; these are totals across multiple designs, not OpenFlexure sales or a monetary revenue figure. The account identified **17 companies** involved with the repository and acknowledged that downstream diffusion was difficult to track. It also describes an INVENIO cloud-service spinout arising from demand for support of CERN open-source *software*: a useful example of service-based transfer, but not a hardware-sales outcome. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028)

## Licensing and how revenue is captured

Open licensing allows manufacture and commercial sale rather than reserving sales to the academic inventors. CERN’s original **Open Hardware Licence** was described as covering use, modification and distribution of design documentation and products made from it, with covered developments shared on the same terms. For a **specific microscope**, Imperial’s openFrame paper expressly identifies its core CAD-file license as **CERN-OHL-P version 2**, the permissive variant, and contemplates incorporation into companies’ commercial instruments. The paper’s own Creative Commons publication license is a different matter. Likewise, an OpenFlexure clinical paper says its **Figure 1** was reproduced under **CC BY-SA**; that caption alone does **not** establish that every OpenFlexure hardware file, software component and trademark has that license. A buyer or manufacturer must check the applicable files and versions rather than infer a project-wide license from an article or figure. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053)

The corresponding business models are **manufacture and quality assurance; kits and hard-to-source components; customization and system integration; and installation, calibration, validation, maintenance and training**. Some are demonstrated above, whereas others are identified in the business-model literature as opportunities, not proven income streams for each named project. Complementary-product sales are another documented strategy: NECi released an open photometer design while selling the enzymes used with it, so additional manufacturers could enlarge demand for its principal product. Open branding and support can also distinguish an original vendor from a cheaper copy. No license, by itself, provides clinical certification or assigns manufacturer responsibility for product quality. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037)

## Barriers to turning a published prototype into a supported product

* **Certification, safety and liability.** Medical certification attaches to a **manufactured, assembled device**, not automatically to an open design. The sayansiScope team described certification as work in progress, requiring documented quality management under **ISO 13485** and risk management under **ISO 14971**. Different builders, components and modifications create calibration and traceability problems; the OpenFlexure team proposed testing each completed microscope, periodically rechecking essential characteristics, recording results and constraining clinical software to approved configurations. Open-source diagnostic assays and equipment still face jurisdictional regulation: an unapproved DIY device cannot simply substitute for a validated clinical system. Responsibility for calibration and conformity can be unclear when designers, builders and users are different parties—precisely the issue a commercial manufacturer or certified laboratory must resolve, rather than a liability that an open license removes. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049)
* **Support and manufacturability.** Early clinician feedback on OpenFlexure found a preference for a device assembled by an **external supplier** and returned to that supplier for maintenance, despite its self-build design. Open projects need sustained documentation, usable interfaces, spare parts and technical assistance after a grant ends. Jubilee’s motion platform comprised **more than 800 components** sourced from over a dozen vendors, and interviewed builders commonly spent months assembling it; its eventual kit addresses a real logistical burden. Procurement rules can also make inexpensive overseas components difficult for universities to buy. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049)
* **Cloning, incentives and finance.** Open designs permit competing copies. The literature documents Arduino clones and discusses branding, warranty, service, rapid iteration and complementary sales as responses; **it does not establish a quantified cloning loss for OpenFlexure or Opentrons**. Lack of exclusive IP may trouble investors, while university patent procedures, limited business-development capacity and the gap between prototype grants and production funding can delay transfer. Conversely, treating every copy as lost revenue would ignore legitimate independent manufacture and the potential for wider adoption. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000037)

**Bottom line.** The literature documents actual firms, supplied components, modest crowdfunded kit batches, clinical-development partnerships and some unit-level outcomes. It rarely reports audited revenue for the named academic-origin microscope and automation companies. The defensible conclusion is therefore that **several commercial routes have been demonstrated**, while reliable product-specific revenue, sustained profitability and—in many cases—formal spinout status remain unverified in the cited record. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000031)"}

Separately, Tanzanian partner Bongo Tech and Research Labs manufactures an OpenFlexure-derived **sayansiScope** and was working toward medical-device certification in the 2024 account. OpenFlexure had been built or used in **more than 45 countries** and had reached **technology-readiness level 7**, including operational testing with patient samples; neither figure is a sales total. The cited material does not establish that either manufacturer is a *formal university spinout*, nor disclose its revenue. Other documented product businesses include Opentrons, openUC2 and Sci-Bots, which is listed for the DropBot digital-microfluidics controller. These are examples of commercialization around open designs, not evidence that all have the same institutional ownership or licensing arrangement. During the COVID-19 response, an account reported an Opentrons-supported workflow developed with diagnostic partners for **up to 2,400 tests per day**, associated with US FDA emergency-use authorization, and reported automation at Barcelona’s Hospital Clínic diagnostic centre. The regulatory claim concerns that testing workflow; it should not be read as approval of every use of an open pipetting robot. An academic lab can also publish a liquid handler without establishing a seller: PHIL, FINDUS and OpenWorkstation document buildable laboratory-automation designs, but their reported prototype or component costs are not evidence of commercial sales. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050)

This documents a stated supplier route, not a measured volume of completed sales. The paper estimates **under £10,000** in components for some self-assembled bright-field or fluorescence configurations and approximately **£35,000** for its motorized easySTORM configuration, excluding a computer; both are *assembly-cost estimates*. Jubilee illustrates a transition from sourcing parts from numerous vendors to a complete kit offered by a US vendor in February 2022. Its **170 independently built machines** by then establish uptake before the kit launch, not 170 kit sales. More generally, LabMaker and Adafruit are identified as vendors of designs developed by others; marketplaces and resellers—including Tindie and, in broader open-hardware examples, MatterHackers and Adafruit—can provide distribution without acquiring exclusive design rights. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

These are unusually transparent *per-kit figures*, not annual revenue. The wider literature identifies crowdfunding as a way to finance pre-sales and test demand, and group purchasing as a means of reducing small-batch production risk; neither guarantees a scalable business. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039)

The account identified **17 companies** involved with the repository and acknowledged that downstream diffusion was difficult to track. # Commercialization of academic open-source laboratory hardware

**The documented pathway is to publish a reproducible design while selling the things that publication does not supply:** manufactured and tested instruments, convenient kits, specialist components, integration, training, and dependable support. Openness permits competing manufacturers; it does not eliminate customers’ willingness to pay for an instrument that works on arrival. Evidence of commercial *activity* is considerably stronger than evidence of company revenue or profit for individual academic projects. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010)

The cases below distinguish reported sales from self-builds, prices, manufacturing costs, and plans.

| Project and institutional origin | Demonstrated commercialization route and named vendor | Exact reported outcome or financial metric | License and caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| **OpenFlexure Microscope** — UK university-led project co-developed with Tanzanian, Cameroonian, Ghanaian and US partners | **OpenFlexure Industries** manufactures the microscope and block stage; **Bongo Tech and Research Labs** manufactures the Tanzanian **sayansiScope**, which is being developed toward medical-device certification. Neither firm should be called a formal university spinout without further evidence. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000045) | Built or used in **more than 45 countries** and at **TRL 7**, including operational testing on patient samples. Medical certification was still **ongoing**, not achieved, in 2024; no sales or revenue figure was reported. (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000054) | Hardware and software permit manufacture, modification, use and sale. The paper’s **CC BY-SA** statement applies specifically to reproduced Figure 1, not demonstrably to the whole project. Compliance work references **ISO 13485** and **ISO 14971**. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055) |
| **Opentrons OT.One/OT-2** — open laboratory-automation platform | Sale of assembled robots and add-ons by **Opentrons**; commercial value rests on a ready-to-use, documented platform rather than exclusive design rights. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000001) | The early **OT.One list price was US$3,000**—a price, not revenue. During COVID-19, an Opentrons platform was reported to automate up to **2,400 tests/day**, contribute to an FDA-EUA-approved workflow and operate at Barcelona’s Hospital Clinic diagnostic centre. No verified company revenue or unit-sales total was found. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000026) | Open-source status is documented, but the reviewed evidence does not establish one project-wide CERN-OHL or CC BY-SA version. Clinical approval covered a testing workflow, not every generic OT-2 use. |
| **Foldscope** — Stanford-origin paper microscope | Mass manufacture and direct distribution/sale; later associated with **Foldscope Instruments/Foldscope Inc.** Federal funding supported the pilot. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Manu Prakash reported **50,000 Foldscopes made and sold** by 2017. “Shipping **one million**” in 2017 and the goal to distribute one million by 2019 were prospective statements, not confirmed sales. Reported production cost was **under US$1**, also not sales revenue. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000017) | The supplied evidence does not verify a project-wide CC BY-SA or CERN-OHL license. Reported quantities must not be conflated: 50,000 was historical sales; one million was a target or projection. |
| **openFrame** — Imperial College London with company co-authors from **Cairn Research Ltd** | University files enable self-manufacture and commercial integration; **Cairn Research** stated it would sell openFrame components to users unwilling to fabricate them. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000023) | A self-assembled bright-field or fluorescence system was estimated at **under £10,000**; a motorized easySTORM system at about **£35,000** excluding computer. These are build costs, not sales or revenue. (pqac-00000023) | Core CAD files use **CERN-OHL-P v2**, expressly permitting companies to incorporate components into commercial instruments. The article itself is CC BY, a separate publication license. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000043) |
| **CLSLab:Light** — University of Utah academic self-driving-lab demonstrator | At-cost kits crowdfunded or pre-sold through **GroupGets** and used in university classrooms. (pqac-00000031) | **Two successful crowdfunding rounds totaling 39 kits**. Stated list price: **US$80 plus shipping**, comprising a US$15.57 platform fee, US$51.19 hardware, about US$6 labor/testing and approximately **US$2.24 profit per kit** before bulk discounts. (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039) | Software is modular and open source; the reviewed evidence does not establish a hardware-license version. This is documented small-batch kit commercialization, not a scaled company or material revenue stream. |
| **Jubilee** — University of Washington open tool-changing platform for liquid handling, fabrication and education | Initially distributed as plans for self-sourcing; specialist vendors sold individual CNC parts, followed by a complete US-vendor kit in February 2022. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038) | At least **170 independently built machines** by February 2022 and a community of **1,870** Discord members. These are self-build and adoption figures, not commercial sales; the first complete kit launched in **February 2022**. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000038) | Version 2.2 received a **Creative Commons 4.0 International** license; the excerpt does not identify the exact CC variant. The case illustrates months-long sourcing, 800+ components and support burdens before kit commercialization. (pqac-00000011) |
| **CERN Open Hardware Repository** — CERN with academic and industrial collaborators | Firms co-develop and manufacture repository designs for CERN and other customers; CERN acts as pilot customer and quality signal. (pqac-00000028) | By the end of 2014, **eight CERN designs** were commercially available and **more than 1,200 units** had been produced for almost **100 users**. This is an aggregate across eight designs—not OpenFlexure sales or revenue. (pqac-00000028) | Most repository projects used **CERN-OHL**, requiring covered developments to be republished under the same terms. The repository had 17 participating companies, but tracking commercial diffusion remained difficult. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028) |
| **UC2 / openUC2** — academic modular microscopy platform | Documented revenue route is **selling hardware as a product** through openUC2; available evidence does not establish formal university-spinout status. (pqac-00000036) | No verified sales, unit or revenue figure was found in the reviewed literature. | Open-hardware status is documented, but no exact project license was verified in the supplied evidence; CERN-OHL should not be inferred merely because UC2 appears in broader licensing discussions. |
| **DropBot** — academic digital-microfluidic system | **Sci-Bots** is listed as the commercial company for the DropBot digital-microfluidic control system. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000041) | No verified sales, price or revenue figure was found in the reviewed evidence. | Commercial availability is documented, but neither a specific license version nor a formal spinout relationship was established by the supplied sources. |


*Table: Comparison of documented commercialization routes, vendors, quantitative outcomes, and licensing caveats for academic-origin open scientific hardware. The table distinguishes confirmed sales from build counts, prices, costs, projections, and aggregate repository figures.*

## Pathways and observed outcomes

**Product companies and local manufacture.** OpenFlexure Industries is listed as a manufacturer of the OpenFlexure microscope and block stage. Separately, Tanzanian partner Bongo Tech and Research Labs manufactures an OpenFlexure-derived **sayansiScope** and was working toward medical-device certification in the 2024 account. OpenFlexure had been built or used in **more than 45 countries** and had reached **technology-readiness level 7**, including operational testing with patient samples; neither figure is a sales total. The cited material does not establish that either manufacturer is a *formal university spinout*, nor disclose its revenue. Other documented product businesses include Opentrons, openUC2 and Sci-Bots, which is listed for the DropBot digital-microfluidics controller. These are examples of commercialization around open designs, not evidence that all have the same institutional ownership or licensing arrangement. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000055)

**Assembled robots and application-specific integration.** An early Opentrons **OT.One was listed at US$3,000**; that is a product price, *not* Opentrons revenue. During the COVID-19 response, an account reported an Opentrons-supported workflow developed with diagnostic partners for **up to 2,400 tests per day**, associated with US FDA emergency-use authorization, and reported automation at Barcelona’s Hospital Clínic diagnostic centre. The regulatory claim concerns that testing workflow; it should not be read as approval of every use of an open pipetting robot. An academic lab can also publish a liquid handler without establishing a seller: PHIL, FINDUS and OpenWorkstation document buildable laboratory-automation designs, but their reported prototype or component costs are not evidence of commercial sales. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000050)

**Kit sellers, component suppliers and distributors.** Imperial College London’s **openFrame** team worked with Cairn Research Ltd; its paper states that Cairn **would sell** openFrame components to users who want to assemble instruments but not fabricate the components. This documents a stated supplier route, not a measured volume of completed sales. The paper estimates **under £10,000** in components for some self-assembled bright-field or fluorescence configurations and approximately **£35,000** for its motorized easySTORM configuration, excluding a computer; both are *assembly-cost estimates*. Jubilee illustrates a transition from sourcing parts from numerous vendors to a complete kit offered by a US vendor in February 2022. Its **170 independently built machines** by then establish uptake before the kit launch, not 170 kit sales. More generally, LabMaker and Adafruit are identified as vendors of designs developed by others; marketplaces and resellers—including Tindie and, in broader open-hardware examples, MatterHackers and Adafruit—can provide distribution without acquiring exclusive design rights. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000040)

**Crowdfunded small batches and educational kits.** The University of Utah’s open **CLSLab:Light** self-driving-laboratory teaching demonstrator went beyond a downloadable design: the authors report **two successful GroupGets rounds totaling 39 kits**, some used in university teaching. Their April 2023 disclosure gives a **US$80 list price plus shipping**, **US$51.19 hardware**, **US$15.57 platform fees**, about **US$6 labor/testing**, and approximately **US$2.24 profit per kit** before the effects of bulk discounts. These are unusually transparent *per-kit figures*, not annual revenue. The wider literature identifies crowdfunding as a way to finance pre-sales and test demand, and group purchasing as a means of reducing small-batch production risk; neither guarantees a scalable business. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000039)

**High-volume manufacture is possible, but projections must stay projections.** Stanford-origin Foldscope provides a different scale of example. Manu Prakash reported in 2017 that **50,000 microscopes had been made and sold**; his statement that the team *would ship one million that year*, and a separately reported million-device distribution goal, are **targets or forecasts**, not independently verified million-unit sales. The reported **less-than-US$1 production cost** likewise is not a sale price or revenue. Federal funding supported its early pilot. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000025)

**Institutional licensing and industry co-development.** The CERN Open Hardware Repository shows a transfer route in which companies help develop or manufacture openly documented designs and the research institution serves as an initial customer and quality signal. CERN reported that, by the end of **2014**, **eight CERN designs were commercially available** and **more than 1,200 units** had been produced for almost **100 users**; these are totals across multiple designs, not OpenFlexure sales or a monetary revenue figure. The account identified **17 companies** involved with the repository and acknowledged that downstream diffusion was difficult to track. It also describes an INVENIO cloud-service spinout arising from demand for support of CERN open-source *software*: a useful example of service-based transfer, but not a hardware-sales outcome. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000028)

## Licensing and how revenue is captured

Open licensing allows manufacture and commercial sale rather than reserving sales to the academic inventors. CERN’s original **Open Hardware Licence** was described as covering use, modification and distribution of design documentation and products made from it, with covered developments shared on the same terms. For a **specific microscope**, Imperial’s openFrame paper expressly identifies its core CAD-file license as **CERN-OHL-P version 2**, the permissive variant, and contemplates incorporation into companies’ commercial instruments. The paper’s own Creative Commons publication license is a different matter. Likewise, an OpenFlexure clinical paper says its **Figure 1** was reproduced under **CC BY-SA**; that caption alone does **not** establish that every OpenFlexure hardware file, software component and trademark has that license. A buyer or manufacturer must check the applicable files and versions rather than infer a project-wide license from an article or figure. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000053)

The corresponding business models are **manufacture and quality assurance; kits and hard-to-source components; customization and system integration; and installation, calibration, validation, maintenance and training**. Some are demonstrated above, whereas others are identified in the business-model literature as opportunities, not proven income streams for each named project. Complementary-product sales are another documented strategy: NECi released an open photometer design while selling the enzymes used with it, so additional manufacturers could enlarge demand for its principal product. Open branding and support can also distinguish an original vendor from a cheaper copy. No license, by itself, provides clinical certification or assigns manufacturer responsibility for product quality. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037)

## Barriers to turning a published prototype into a supported product

* **Certification, safety and liability.** Medical certification attaches to a **manufactured, assembled device**, not automatically to an open design. The sayansiScope team described certification as work in progress, requiring documented quality management under **ISO 13485** and risk management under **ISO 14971**. Different builders, components and modifications create calibration and traceability problems; the OpenFlexure team proposed testing each completed microscope, periodically rechecking essential characteristics, recording results and constraining clinical software to approved configurations. Open-source diagnostic assays and equipment still face jurisdictional regulation: an unapproved DIY device cannot simply substitute for a validated clinical system. Responsibility for calibration and conformity can be unclear when designers, builders and users are different parties—precisely the issue a commercial manufacturer or certified laboratory must resolve, rather than a liability that an open license removes. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049)
* **Support and manufacturability.** Early clinician feedback on OpenFlexure found a preference for a device assembled by an **external supplier** and returned to that supplier for maintenance, despite its self-build design. Open projects need sustained documentation, usable interfaces, spare parts and technical assistance after a grant ends. Jubilee’s motion platform comprised **more than 800 components** sourced from over a dozen vendors, and interviewed builders commonly spent months assembling it; its eventual kit addresses a real logistical burden. Procurement rules can also make inexpensive overseas components difficult for universities to buy. (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049)
* **Cloning, incentives and finance.** Open designs permit competing copies. The literature documents Arduino clones and discusses branding, warranty, service, rapid iteration and complementary sales as responses; **it does not establish a quantified cloning loss for OpenFlexure or Opentrons**. Lack of exclusive IP may trouble investors, while university patent procedures, limited business-development capacity and the gap between prototype grants and production funding can delay transfer. Conversely, treating every copy as lost revenue would ignore legitimate independent manufacture and the potential for wider adoption. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000037)

**Bottom line.** The literature documents actual firms, supplied components, modest crowdfunded kit batches, clinical-development partnerships and some unit-level outcomes. It rarely reports audited revenue for the named academic-origin microscope and automation companies. The defensible conclusion is therefore that **several commercial routes have been demonstrated**, while reliable product-specific revenue, sustained profitability and—in many cases—formal spinout status remain unverified in the cited record. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000031)

contexts.context: Jubilee demonstrates an academic/open project progressing from self-sourcing to commercial kit sales. Its 800+ component design required fabrication and purchases from over a dozen vendors; builders reported months-long assembly, with shipping the main obstacle (“Every time I got stuck was actually due to shipping issues”). A Creative Commons 4.0 license was added in December 2020. Community Discord support—questions often answered within seconds—helped overcome documentation and assembly challenges. At least 170 machines were built by February 2022, when version 2.2.2 became a complete U.S.-vendor-supplied kit, ending the exclusively self-built phase.

contexts.context: Open hardware commercialization benefits from transparent CAD files, modular designs, GitHub collaboration, community validation, and low-cost distributed manufacturing (including 3D printing and makerspaces). Open development can lower marketing costs through word of mouth and community showcases, while enabling derivative products and supply-chain adaptation. However, commercialization requires calibration, documentation, standards, and regulatory compliance; unclear responsibility among designers, manufacturers, and users can impede trust and adoption. PPE made in makerspaces was rejected by hospitals when standards could not be demonstrated, whereas Make4COVID and Helpful Engineering used standards-based assessment and regulatory-grade partnerships.

contexts.context: Commercialization can involve selling finished tools or kits, consumer sales, customer support, education/training, and outsourced research services. Open communities generally accept commercialization when designs are innovative, while expecting contributions back through licensing, documentation, certification, and community assessment (e.g., DIN SPEC 3105 and Open Know How metadata). contexts.context: CERN commercializes academic technologies through service/consultancy agreements, collaborations, licenses, and spinouts. Demand for its open-source INVENIO software led to a spin-off delivering it as a cloud service; consultancy also supports specialized CERN equipment and software such as INDICO. CERN favors open source, recommending GPLv3 (or LGPLv3/Apache v2), while the CERN Open Hardware Licence (CERN-OHL) permits studying, modifying, using, producing, and distributing designs, provided derivatives are shared under the same terms. Reported exceptions include inadequate packaging or quality, external funding constraints, or cases where proprietary licensing would better maximize dissemination; CERN notes limited ability to track open-source impact.

contexts.context: CERN’s Open Hardware Repository uses the CERN OHL and hosts 100+ projects, with 17 companies involved. CERN acts as a pilot customer, legitimizing quality and helping firms sell elsewhere. By late 2014, eight commercially available CERN designs had produced “more than 1200 units” for “almost 100 different users.” Commercialization includes firms manufacturing hardware, preferential licensing, consultancy/partnerships, and BIC incubation offering expertise, networks, financing access and office space. Spinouts remained limited—only two agreements in 2014—though former staff, students and fellows also formed informal spinouts. Tracking dissemination and impact remains difficult.

contexts.context: Jubilee (released 2019) demonstrates distributed, self-produced open hardware rather than academic commercialization: a tool-changing machine built from off-the-shelf and digitally fabricated parts. Researchers documented “170+ Jubilees built in the wild,” interviewing 12 builders and analyzing GitHub, Discord, and Wiki. Self-production was challenging but viable, enabling customization and design improvement through community feedback. The article contrasts this with companies such as Arduino, Beagleboard, Prusa, Ultimaker, Seeed Studio, and DFRobot, which generally centralize production and sales. It identifies manufacturing cost, specialist expertise, reliable sourcing, quality control, and niche-market economics as barriers; crowdfunding suits high-growth products more than low-volume hardware.

contexts.context: The excerpt recommends commercialization pathways including group-buy/kit distributors such as GroupGets and partnerships with organizations like Veterans Affairs that can manufacture in regulatory-grade environments. It identifies funding gaps between concept and production, noting investors may view open hardware’s lack of conventional IP as risky. Suggested supports include legal/IP training, commercialization funds, and NSF I-Corps entrepreneurship mentoring. Designers often lack business and marketing expertise. Small-batch or DIY tools may remain at the concept stage because engineering, validation, certification, standards alignment, and regulatory compliance are incomplete. Open standards and accessible certification guidelines are proposed to improve scalability and credibility.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on educational, low-cost self-driving laboratories (SDLs), not commercialization. It argues that affordability and accessibility require schematics, parts lists, assembly instructions, code documentation, and troubleshooting guides to overcome financial and technical barriers. Examples include automated titrators supporting disability-inclusive chemistry education and CLSLab:Light, a modular light-mixing SDL costing under **$100**, requiring **under an hour** to set up, minimal space, and no chemical consumables. It mentions open liquid handlers (including Opentrons OT-2 and OpenLH) but gives no spinout, seller, distributor, revenue, crowdfunding, licensing, certification, liability, support, or cloning outcomes.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Opentrons as an open-source academic/community lab-automation platform commercialized through partnerships: with BP Genomics and the Open Medicine Institute it targeted automation of up to **2,400 tests/day**, pursued **FDA Emergency Use Authorization**, and automated COVID-19 testing at Barcelona’s Hospital Clinic. Other pathways included Chai Bio’s **Open qPCR environmental kit**, distributed reproduction of protocols via OpenCOVID/Just One Giant Lab, and open biological-resource initiatives. Barriers included certification, FDA/CDC validation, regulated manufacture/use, proprietary cartridges and tips, and dependence on emergency approval schemes. Licenses across related projects included **CERN-OHL v2.0, GPL, MIT, and CC-BY-NC**.

contexts.context: CLSLab:Light illustrates an academic-to-market pathway: modular, open-source software, build instructions, video tutorials, and supply-chain-resilient parts lists support replication and adaptation (including CLSLab:Liquid). Baird and Sparks explored selling it as an at-cost kit through GroupGets; two crowdfunding campaigns (#1112, #1129) succeeded, totaling 39 kits, many used in university classrooms. The platform’s modularity enables domain-specific extensions and integration with systems such as Opentrons. The excerpt emphasizes educational/community uptake rather than spinout companies, revenue, licensing terms beyond the article’s CC BY 3.0 status, or documented certification, liability, support, and cloning barriers.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents open hardware as commercially viable through selling components/kits, complete instruments, and specialized equipment. SparkFun reports US$32 million annual revenue and 146 employees; Adafruit exceeds US$45 million; Arduino is owned by Qualcomm (US$44 billion annual revenue). OpenTrons’ open-source liquid-handling robots reportedly displace proprietary systems costing ten times more. Backyard Brains commercialized peer-reviewed open neuroscience hardware, while NASA-engineer spinout re:3D and MatterHackers built businesses around RepRap. LulzBot sells open-source printers and bioprinters. Collectively, such firms employ thousands and generate hundreds of millions annually from openly licensed designs. No crowdfunding, CERN-OHL/CC BY-SA, service models, or barriers are detailed.

It stresses sustainability, industrial adoption, legal/ethical issues, and support. OpenFlexure is an openly documented, 3D-printed, laboratory-grade microscope intended for research, education, and medical use; commercial microscopes cost about £20,000 plus maintenance. Medical commercialization requires version control, design-risk assessment, documentation, and manufacturers understanding design history. Open licensing enables use, modification, and selling copies, but openness is “not necessarily cheap.”

contexts.context: Open hardware can commercialize through direct sales plus open licensing, “secondary supplier” sales that expand complementary markets, or services. NECi open-sourced a low-cost photometer to increase enzyme sales; cloners broaden reach and may benefit the primary business. Service pathways include subscriptions/service contracts, memberships, installation, maintenance, support, training, books, workshops, certification and consulting; Open Source Ecology charges for workshops. Firms can out-innovate clones (SparkFun) or rely on services. OSHWA certification addresses misleading “Open Source” claims. The excerpt notes cloning can undercut hardware prices, threatening firms dependent solely on hardware revenue.

contexts.context: openFrame is an academically developed, low-cost modular microscope combining self-built/open-source and proprietary commercial components. CAD files and manufacturing resources are freely shared via GitHub under CERN Open Hardware License v2; the paper explicitly invites companies to incorporate openFrame components into commercial instruments or attach commercial modules. The platform is supported by UK/US research grants and collaborations with Cairn Research Ltd, but reports no sales, revenue, crowdfunding, spinout, kit seller, distributor, or service model. Its stated rationale is reducing instrument cost/development time and widening access, rather than documenting commercialization barriers or outcomes.

contexts.context: The academic self-driving-lab demo is commercialized mainly through reproducible DIY kits and component distribution rather than a spinout. Authors explored selling at-cost kits via GroupGets crowdfunding: as of April 23, 2023, list price was $80 plus shipping; GroupGets fee $15.57, hardware $51.19, labor/testing $6, leaving only $2.24 profit. Users source parts through DigiKey, Adafruit, CanaKit, PiHut, or ElectroMaker, while code is openly hosted on GitHub/Zenodo. Documented practical barriers include component stockouts, incompatible parts, soldering, SD-card failures, Wi-Fi setup, database-logging issues, and reliance on issue trackers and community support.

contexts.context: RepRap illustrates decentralized self-production: users make most parts, while commercial centrally produced printers expand reach but reduce customization; kits offer an intermediate model. Its Marlin firmware became a de facto standard used by Prusa, Lulzbot, Ultimaker, Ender/CR, and research machines. Jubilee, an academic/open project released in 2019 for customizable tool-changing, 3D-printing and liquid-handling, emphasized “fabricatability” and extensibility, enabling makers to source or produce components. Its community grew from 570 to 1,870 members (2020–2022); on February 10, 2022, Jubilee became a kit, ending its exclusively self-produced phase.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background on CERN’s open-hardware model but does not identify the specific academic-origin instruments or companies requested, including openFrame/Cairn, CLSLab GroupGets, OpenFlexure, or Opentrons. It confirms that the CERN Open Hardware Repository hosts more than 100 projects and that the CERN OHL has been adopted by companies, research institutions, and individuals beyond high-energy physics. It also reports that, by the end of 2014, eight commercially available CERN designs had produced more than 1,200 units for almost 100 users. This is a sales/output figure, not a build-cost figure, although the passage does not provide prices, revenues, margins, or per-instrument sales. The excerpt does not specify whether individual instruments use CERN-OHL-P, CERN-OHL-S, or CC BY-SA; it only refers generally to the CERN OHL. It contains no crowdfunding-kit results, verified liability or safety barriers, or evidence concerning cloning. The passage does note that measuring open-hardware dissemination and impact remains difficult. CERN’s repository therefore offers relevant context for licensing and commercialization, but the requested company-level comparisons and safety, licensing-variant, crowdfunding, and cloning claims require other sources.

contexts.context: OpenFlexure’s academic prototype is progressing toward healthcare deployment rather than describing sales. It reached Technology Readiness Level 7, operating in Tanzanian clinics for patient blood samples and at a Texas VA center for biopsies. Commercialization/adoption requires manufacturing-ready designs, technical documentation, ongoing support, clinician acceptance, testing, feedback and co-development with Mboalab, Bongo Tech and Baylor College of Medicine. OpenFlexure Connect lowers barriers by replacing Git/Jupyter/Linux workflows with guided calibration, autofocus, scanning and locked, medically approved modes. ISO 13485 alignment is identified as important for medical effectiveness; accessibility also depends on translations and retaining the original core team.

contexts.context: OpenFlexure began as a 2016 academic project and is open source: users may “manufacture, use, modify and sell” hardware/software without patent or copyright restrictions. International uptake has produced spin-out projects such as the OpenFlexure Block Stage and Delta Stage, while other groups adapted it for super-resolution and optical-sectioning microscopy. The proposed pathway toward medical deployment emphasizes local manufacture, maintenance and use in remote settings rather than donation, which often fails because of consumables, spare parts, maintenance and training needs. The excerpt focuses on technical/social challenges, not revenues, crowdfunding, distributors, licensing variants or sales figures.

contexts.context: OpenFlexure’s excerpt emphasizes infrastructure needed before commercialization: medical certification requires an auditable archive of design decisions, while Git/GitLab tracks CAD, software, calibration and evolving variants. GitBuilding automates bills of materials and shared documentation. Diverse clinical requirements force trade-offs among speed, reliability, customization, quality, cost and supply-chain accessibility; narrowly scoped diagnostic applications may build confidence before broader laboratory use. The project ultimately aims for users to adopt devices “without direct support from the core team,” but private communications risk lost decisions and duplicated work. No spinout, sales, licensing, crowdfunding or revenue figures are reported here.

contexts.context: This excerpt addresses the organizational, documentation, accessibility, and clinical-development context of the OpenFlexure project. It states that medical certification requires an archived record of design decisions so the project history can be traced. Git and GitLab are used to version-control both software and microscope CAD files, with GitLab preferred for public discussion, archiving, traceability, and openness. GitBuilding supports documentation of multiple microscope variants by tracking parts, generating bills of materials, and linking shared build instructions. The paper emphasizes that accessibility depends on reducing barriers in the supply chain, documentation, and software, and that component choices must balance image quality against cost and availability. It also describes the longer-term goal of a generic laboratory device, while initially focusing on a narrower set of diagnostic tests, primarily malaria diagnosis in blood samples. The project ultimately aims for users to adopt the technology without direct support from the core team. However, the supplied pages do not provide the requested exact CC-BY-SA context, sayansiScope local-manufacturing information, certification status, ISO 13485 or ISO 14971 details, deployment in 45 countries, TRL 7 classification, clinician preference for a supported external supplier, Figure 1 licensing distinctions, commercial-vendor information, or revenue figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents that Figure 1 is an exploded-view artwork reproduced from reference [1] under a CC-BY-SA licence; this statement applies specifically to the figure and does not establish the licensing terms for the entire OpenFlexure project. It identifies sayansiScope as the OpenFlexure Microscope manufactured in Tanzania by Bongo Tech and Research Labs, with work ongoing toward medical certification. The authors state that certification applies to an assembled product rather than to the underlying design. The relevant quality-management framework named here is ISO 13485, which requires systematic consideration of a device’s applications, limits, and risks and documentation across its full lifecycle. This excerpt does not mention ISO 14971, deployment or use in 45 countries, a Technology Readiness Level of 7, clinician preference for a supported external supplier, a commercial vendor beyond Bongo Tech and Research Labs, or any revenue figures.
